cards.front: Show the maximum number of open file descriptors allowed in your current shell
cards.back: `ulimit -n`

cards.front: A 30 GB deleted log is still held open by process 1234 as file descriptor 4, and you can't restart the process. How do you free the space?
cards.back: Truncate it through `/proc`: `: > /proc/1234/fd/4`

cards.front: Why does `cmd 2>&1 > log.txt` still print errors to the terminal?
cards.back: Redirections run left to right, so stderr copied stdout while stdout was still the terminal. Use `cmd > log.txt 2>&1`.

cards.front: Why does a Python script's `print` output appear in `app.log` only much later when run as `python app.py > app.log`?
cards.back: stdout sent to a file is buffered in blocks, not lines; run `python -u app.py` to write immediately.

cards.front: List the file descriptors that process 1234 has open, and where each one points
cards.back: `ls -l /proc/1234/fd`

cards.front: Your small script pushes the server out of memory, but the out-of-memory killer kills the database instead. Why?
cards.back: It kills the process with the highest `oom_score`, which is mostly the largest memory user, not the process that asked for memory.

cards.front: A process died with code `137`. Check whether the out-of-memory killer was responsible.
cards.back: `sudo dmesg -T | grep -i 'killed process'`

cards.front: After logrotate runs `copytruncate`, `ls -l app.log` still shows 10 GB, but `du -h app.log` shows only a few KB. What happened?
cards.back: The app didn't open the log in append mode. It kept writing at its old offset, which left a sparse file with a hole at the start.

cards.front: logrotate runs with its default `create` mode. Afterwards the new `app.log` stays empty while `app.log.1` keeps growing. What went wrong?
cards.back: The app still holds the old file open, now named `app.log.1`. Make it reopen its log: signal it in `postrotate` (often `SIGHUP`), or restart it.

cards.front: Repoint the existing symlink `current` (to a directory) at `releases/v2` instead of creating a link inside it
cards.back: `ln -sfn releases/v2 current`

cards.front: A nightly job exits with code `137`. Can you conclude that the out-of-memory killer killed it?
cards.back: No. `137` means the process died from SIGKILL. The OOM killer sends SIGKILL, and so does anyone running `kill -9`.

cards.front: A Python script loading a huge CSV never raises `MemoryError`. It just dies with `Killed`. Why?
cards.back: Linux overcommits memory. The allocation usually succeeds, and when RAM really runs out, the kernel kills a process instead.

cards.front: Why does `sudo echo hi > /etc/myconf` fail with Permission denied?
cards.back: Your own non-root shell opens the file for `>` before `sudo` runs. Use `echo hi | sudo tee /etc/myconf`.

cards.front: Your Python script deletes its temp files in a `finally:` block. After an out-of-memory kill, the temp files are still there. Why?
cards.back: The `finally:` block never ran. The process stopped instantly and executed none of its remaining code.

cards.front: Why does `ln /data/file /mnt/ebs/file` fail with "Invalid cross-device link"?
cards.back: A hard link points to an inode number, which only means something inside one filesystem.

cards.front: `app.conf` and `backup.conf` are hard links to the same file. After `sed -i 's/a/b/' app.conf`, does `backup.conf` change?
cards.back: No, `sed -i` writes a new file with a new inode, so `backup.conf` keeps the old content.

cards.front: In logrotate, what is the trade-off between `create` (the default) and `copytruncate`?
cards.back: `create` needs the app to reopen its log. `copytruncate` needs nothing from the app, but it can lose lines.

cards.front: `df -h` says `/` is 95% full, but `du -sh /` adds up to much less. What is the usual cause?
cards.back: Deleted files that a running process still holds open. `df` counts their blocks, but `du` cannot see them.

cards.front: The disk shows free space in `df -h`, yet writes fail with "No space left on device". What do you check next?
cards.back: `df -i`, because the filesystem may have run out of inodes, often from millions of tiny files.

cards.front: You deleted a 50 GB log file with `rm`, but `df` shows no space freed. Why?
cards.back: A running process still has the file open, so its inode is kept until the process closes it.
